lesson_title: Measure a River With a String
hook_text: How do you measure a road that twists like spaghetti? You need one thing from your sewing kit.
clip_script: A ruler only measures straight lines. But roads bend, rivers loop and mountain passes zigzag. So geographers use string. Thin cotton, never stretchy wool. Hold one end on the start. Now lay the string along every curve, slowly, pressing it down as you go. Pinch it at the finish. Straighten it out and lay it on the map's scale bar, starting at zero. Once across the bar, five hundred metres. Then three hundred more. Eight hundred metres along that winding road, even though the straight line was only five hundred. That gap is the price of the bends, and it's why a tunnel or a footbridge can save people so much time.
visual_style: A whiteboard winding road; a thread being laid along each curve; the thread pulled straight and laid along a scale bar; then a straight dashed crow line beside it for comparison.
call_to_action: Watch the full lesson and measure any winding route.
